newsitem.title: USA: Weld to be U.S. ambassador to Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Weld to be U.S. ambassador to Mexico.

text.p: Massachusetts Gov. William Weld, who had been seen as a potential challenger to Al Gore in the 2000 presidential elections, will join the Clinton Administration as ambassador to Mexico, his staff said on Sunday.
Weld, a moderate Republican, will replace James Jones, who had been president of the American Stock Exchange before being assigned to the sensitive ambassadorship.
Weld will be succeeded as Massachusetts Governor by the state's Lieutenant Governer, Paul Cellucci, who announced the changes while in Los Angeles on a mission to attract film-makers to his state.
"He has accepted the appointment," Cellucci told reporters. "Given the issues we have with Mexico and Weld's background, I think he is uniquely qualified for the job."

Weld, who was vacationing and preparing to attend the President's Summit on Volunteerism in Philadelphia, was unable to comment. His press secretary, however, said the new post could become official as early as this week.

Weld, who speaks some Spanish but is said not to be fluent, was a supporter of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) linking the U.S., Canada and Mexico. He last worked in Washington as an assistant attorney general at the Justice Department where he headed the criminal division and emphasised narcotics and public corruption. He left in 1988 after two years.

Weld's exit from the governor's office heightens the competition in the 1998 race for Massachusetts Governor. Cellucci and State Treasurer Joseph Malone are seen as the main rivals for the Republican nomination, while Representative Joseph Kennedy is the presumptive favourite for the Democratic nomination.

Asked about that contest, Cellucci declined a direct comment, but said as governor he intended to push forward Weld's agenda of cutting taxes, ridding the government of bureaucracy, promoting education and fighting violence.
"Bill Weld and I have a common vision and a similar political ideology," Cellucci said. He said his administration would continue to push "the agenda that Bill Weld and I have established."
